original_question: How fast can you hit a speed bump while driving and live?
short_answer_summary: A small bump's direct jolt can be survivable at surprisingly high speed, but vehicle damage, loss of control and aerodynamic lift become decisive.
detailed_scientific_explanation: The answer distinguishes an isolated bump impulse from the resulting crash. Tires and suspension absorb many small-bump shocks; even if components fail, the occupant need not suffer a fatal vertical jolt. Typical bumps of 3–4 inches are comparable to tire cushioning, so the rim may not strike. Documented injuries disproportionately involve hard bus seats and bad roads. Larger humps or speed tables differ. At artificially increased car speeds, drag rises with speed squared and lift can overcome weight. A typical sedan might lift off and tumble around 150–300 mph before reaching the bump. Holding it down would expose body panels to destructive winds; still faster motion leads to heating and disassembly. The final 0.9c speeding-ticket calculation is a joke, not a survivable scenario.
initial_assumptions: Typical sedan and small speed bump
Magical propulsion used beyond ordinary top speed
Direct jolt distinguished from control-loss crash

quantitative_facts.value: Typical bump 3–4 in; sedan top speed ~120 mph
Fastest modern cars around 200 mph in source; aerodynamic lift discussed around 200 mph
150–300 mph typical-sedan liftoff range; joke $1.14 billion penalty at 90% light speed
